# Design

**Open by asking: "how will we know this stage is finished?"**

The answer must be an action: *"I handed the four answers to an agent and it
built the narrow path without asking me anything."* Not "the design is clear".
Not "I wrote it down".

Every question the implementer has to ask is a hole in the design. Counting the
questions is the only measurement this stage has. Take it.

## This stage is four conversations, not four documents

One question per turn. State your recommended answer first, so they can agree or
correct instead of composing prose. Each answer becomes **one block in one file**.
If the whole thing takes more than twenty minutes, it is being over-built.

Ask by trigger, not by product size. "It's small" is not a reason to skip
anything — a small tool that sends one email has the same irreversible action as
a large one.

| Question | Ask it when | Skip it and say so when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. What is the shape of the flow? | Always | Never |
| 2. What must it refuse? | Always | Never |
| 3. What may it do without asking? | It can send, write, delete, pay, or publish | It only reads and shows |
| 4. What does the model see when it acts? | The model chooses at runtime which tool to call | The flow is fixed and calls one thing |

Two never-skipped, two by trigger. Write the skipped ones down with the reason —
in three months "I skipped it" and "I never considered it" are the same memory.

## Question 1 — the shape of the flow

Not an architecture diagram. A numbered list with one split in it: which steps are
**fixed, same every time**, and which steps need **judgement at runtime**.

The count of judgement points is the number to watch. Zero or one: this is a
pipeline and it will be cheap, fast and easy to check. Three or more: either the
product genuinely needs to improvise, or the thinking is not finished and the
model is being asked to do it for you.

**Write each judgement point down and name it. The number is the length of that
list, not a separate answer.** The first version asked only for a count, and a count
cannot be argued with: in the first real run the two people disagreed about whether a
case was a judgement call or a rule, and there was nothing to point at, because no list
had ever been produced. Two people can agree on "three" while meaning different threes.

The list is also what settles the disagreement. A judgement point earns its place by
having no rule. Write the rule you think covers it, then try to break it with a real
case: if the rule holds, it is a fixed step; if you can construct a case that beats the
rule, that case is the judgement point — and now you can name it.

Retype, summarise, extract, format, route by a rule — all fixed. Decide which of
five sources is authoritative, judge whether a claim is substantiated, choose
which of three tactics fits this customer — these are judgement. If they cannot
tell which side a step is on, it is judgement wearing a fixed step's clothes, and
it will behave differently every run.

That count is also the honest answer to "should this be an agent at all". A flow
with no judgement points does not need a model choosing its own steps; it needs a
script with one model call inside it — cheaper, faster, and far easier to check.
Say so when it is true. The need stage already asked whether a person would pay for this;
this question asks whether the model needs to be in charge of the order.

## Question 2 — what it must refuse

Two kinds of row, and both are needed:

- **Out of scope.** This product is not for that. "Someone asks it to write the
  final legal wording — it points to a person instead."
- **Would cause harm.** Doing it breaks something: a claim the brand cannot
  prove, a person's data leaving, an action with no undo.

Each row has a fixed shape: **a concrete input → what it must do instead.**

> "Asks whether the serum cures acne → must say it cannot make medical claims,
> and offer the appearance-wording alternative."

If they cannot name a concrete input, it is a value, not a refusal. "Be honest",
"don't be harmful", "stay on brand" are values. Values cannot be tested at the verify stage
and will be quietly dropped when the checks get written. Ask for the input.

**Then ask where the list comes from.** Three answers, and only two are simple:

- **It exists in one place.** Use it.
- **It does not exist at all.** Stop — that is the disconfirming condition from the
  need stage, and the first work is writing the policy, not building the product.
- **It exists, scattered across several places** — a template in the platform's back
  office, three internal threads, and what the supervisor says out loud. This is the
  common case, and the method had no room for it: the need stage only asks whether the
  policy exists, and this question assumes the answer is usable. The missing work is
  *consolidating it*, nobody owns that, and it spans sessions — so it is a ticket, and
  **this block is blocked until it is done.** Say that plainly rather than writing the
  list from memory: a refusal list assembled from what everyone remembers is values with
  arrows drawn on.

The exit condition for this question: **each row can become a check.** If a row
cannot be written as "given this input, that output must not appear", it is not a
refusal yet.

**Most of what they want to write here is not a refusal, and it belongs in the next
question.** A refusal is a prohibition: something the product does not do. A row that says
*how it answers* is a rule, not a refusal. Say so and move the row.

In the first real run, ten of the eleven rows were answer instructions filed under a heading
that said "what it must refuse". Implemented to the name, the row saying "a three-month-old
cannot use this, and do not advise" would have become an escalation — when it explicitly
says not to escalate. This question should end up short. If it has ten rows, look again.

This is also the one place where the design and verify stages overlap on purpose.
Design writes the list; verify turns it into checks. That is not duplication — it is the
list being born with somewhere to go.

## Question 3 — how is each case answered

A different artifact from the last one, and the difference is the shape: question two is a
list of prohibitions, this is a **table**, one row per case the product will actually meet.

| 具体输入 | 该怎么答 | 升级档次 | 依据 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| the buyer's words | what it does, in as many steps as it needs | 不升级 / 软升级 / 硬升级 | which policy clause |

**升级档次 has three values, and one rule:** `不升级` produces the answer; `软升级` produces it
and marks it for a person; `硬升级` does not produce it at all. Name them once, at the top of
the record, and do not let a second word for the same state creep in — the first real run used
five words for these three values, in a document that contained a section about not confusing
two of them.

**Separate the mechanism from the result.** Escalation is what happens to *this case*; the
record's overall state is what the whole thing ends up as, and it is the heaviest case that
decides it. A hard escalation on one case does **not** suppress the others — treating it that
way is how a message asking for a refund *and* reporting a rash ends up with no reply to the
refund, which is the part the person most needed.

**The test for this table: can you write a real buyer message for every row?** A row you
cannot instantiate is a value with columns drawn around it.

**And one constraint no other question has: every row's 该怎么答 must be something the action
permissions allow.** Check the table against question four, row by row. Three rounds of the
first real run kept finding the same defect — a row demanding an action the permission table
did not contain, with nothing to catch it, because the questions are answered separately and
only the exit test ever compares them.

## Question 4 — what it may do without asking

Sort by **whether it can be undone**, never by how important it feels. Importance
is a judgement they will get wrong; reversibility is a fact they can look up.

| Tier | Test | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reversible | If it is wrong, you undo it in one step and nobody saw | Let it act |
| Costly but bounded | Undoable, but it costs money, reaches a person, or is visible for a while | Let it act, record it, cap it |
| Irreversible | Cannot be undone, or was seen by an audience | **Ask a human first** |

The middle tier is the one that gets skipped, and it is where the real damage
lives: not a wrong answer, but fifty wrong answers sent before anyone looked. Put
a number on it — how many, how much, per what period — because "reasonable use"
is not a limit.

Then the sentence that goes in the prompt, in their words: *"Anything in the third
tier stops and asks. Anything in the middle tier does it and tells me after."*

## Question 5 — what the model sees when it acts

For each thing the model can do, three lines:

1. **What it does** — one sentence, in the user's terms.
2. **When not to use it** — mandatory, even if it reads "no exception yet".
3. **What it returns when it fails** — so the model can tell "retry" from "stop".

The second line is the one everyone omits and the one that causes the misuse.
A description that only says what a tool does is permission to use it everywhere.
The most common failure in agent products is not a broken tool; it is a correct
tool used in the wrong situation, and it looks completely normal in the logs.

The third line decides whether a failure costs one step or the whole run. A tool
that fails with an unreadable error teaches the model nothing; a tool that says
"this id does not exist, do not retry with the same id" ends the loop by itself.

Frame it for them: this text is not documentation, it is the model's only view of
the world. Whatever is not written there does not exist for it.

## Question 6 — what the person receives, in each outcome

**This one was missing, and the design exit test found it.** Four blocks were handed to
an agent with instructions to implement the narrowest path; its guesses clustered on one
question — what does the output actually look like. Not what the product does; what the
person is holding when it stops.

Write one line per way the flow can end. For most products that is three or four:

- **It goes through** — what they get, and what makes it usable as-is.
- **Something in it crossed a line** — what they get, and how the crossed part is marked.
- **A piece has no basis** — what happens to that piece, and whether the rest survives.
- **It refuses, or hands off** — what they get *instead*, and what a person needs in order
  to take over. "It refuses" without an artifact is where products quietly become useless:
  the work disappears and nobody can tell what happened.

The test is blunt: point at any outcome and ask **"and what do I get?"** If the answer is
"it just doesn't do it", that outcome produces nothing a person can act on.

If this feels like it belongs to the build stage, note what actually happened: the first
real run produced twelve separate guesses here, and half of them were about the shape of
the output rather than the shape of the logic. The design stage is where that gets
decided, because everything downstream reads it.

## What this stage produces

One file, six blocks, whether or not a block is used:

```
## 一、流程形状      固定步骤 / 需要临场判断的步骤 / 判断点共几处
## 二、拒绝清单      only prohibitions. Short — if it has ten rows, look again
## 三、应答规则      一张决策表：每个具体输入 → 该怎么答 / 升级档次 / 依据
## 四、动作权限      每条动作标一档：可撤销 / 有额度 / 必须问人
## 五、交接契约      每个工具三行：做什么 / 什么时候别用 / 失败返回什么
## 六、产出形态      这条流程有几种结局，每种结局下人拿到手的是什么
```

Plus two lines that cost nothing and save a rewrite:

- **What would make this design wrong** — one observable event, not "if it
  doesn't work". A design with no re-open condition becomes untouchable in three
  months because nobody remembers what it assumed.
- **Which ADRs this produced** — a pointer, not a copy. Hard-to-reverse choices go
  to `docs/adr/`; this record just says which ones.

## Paying for the decision

Two questions separate a choice worth twenty minutes from one worth none:

- **How much does changing it later cost?** If the answer is "an afternoon", decide
  now and move on. Do not design it twice.
- **Can I tell which is better before building?** If no, pick the one that is
  easier to undo and write down what you expect to see.

For a choice that is expensive and genuinely undecidable, describe two shapes and
write, for each, the situation in which it wins. Then pick the one that is cheaper
to back out of. Never pick the more familiar one — familiarity is not evidence.

## How this stage fakes success

**The design becomes a specification.** Forty pages, every edge case, reads
impressively. Test: can you point at one sentence and say "I cannot do that"? If
every line is agreeable, it is a document, not a design.

**The refusal list becomes values.** "Honest", "harmless", "on brand". All true,
none testable. Test: name one input that would trigger each row. No input, no row.

**Permission is sorted by importance.** "Payments are important, so ask before
paying. Reading files is minor, so allow it." Now a read that dumps every customer
record is allowed and a $2 charge is blocked. Test: sort by undo, nothing else.

**The handover contract only says what the tool does.** The model then calls it in
situations it was never meant for, and every log line looks correct.

**The design freezes too early.** It was written before any code existed, so it is
a guess. That is fine — but only if the file says which assumption would break it.
Without that line, the guess becomes a constraint, and later evidence loses to it.

## The thing that goes wrong here

**They will want to skip it**, and the reason will sound reasonable: "this one is
small". The size of the product is not the test. Two facts are:

- Is there any action that cannot be undone?
- Will someone other than the author use it?

Neither: skip the whole stage, write one line saying why. Either one: it is not
small in the way that matters, and question 2 is not optional.

**Do not write this file for them.** Same trap as the need stage, higher cost: a design
you wrote reads better than one they wrote, so they will approve it, and then at
the verify stage there is no standard they can judge against — because the standard is
yours and they cannot see its edges.

Your job is to ask, and to notice when an answer is a value pretending to be a
refusal. Say so, give two concrete options, make them pick.

## What you record

The four blocks go in `work/designs/drafting/D-NNN-slug.md`. When all four are
answered, move it to `confirmed` — that is what turns it from a document into a
spec the verify stage can read.

Four sections, skips marked with a reason, and the condition that would make this
design wrong. `work check` fails a record missing any of them, and fails a confirmed
one that cannot say what would overturn it.

**While the record is in `drafting`, a missing block is fine.** This stage is answered
one question at a time, so a block you have not reached yet is not an omission. But a
block that *exists* is held to the rules from the moment you write it, `drafting`
included: an empty block, or a refusal list whose rows name no concrete input, fails
immediately. Only the four-blocks-present requirement waits for `confirmed`.

## Exit test

They hand the blocks to an agent — **one that can see nothing else**. If that cannot be
arranged, the run is **partially verified**: write down what could not be excluded, and count
the result as evidence about the material rather than about the design. The router already
uses this rule when an exit test needs someone the person does not have; this is the same
situation. In the first real run the agent had tools, read the repository, and reported that
it had — which made the round's numbers mean something different from the next round's.

Then ask it for **two** things, and the second is the one that matters:

1. **How many things did you have to guess?**
2. **Which blocks contradict each other?** Name the pairs.

**Both must be empty.** A design with zero guesses and one cross-block contradiction is not
nearly done — it is a design whose parts do not fit, and everything downstream inherits the
seam. Three rounds of the first real run gave 12/6, 8/9 and 7/7; every hard contradiction was
cross-block, and a count alone would have shown the third round as progress.

Two rounds is normal; more than three means the blocks are wrong, not underspecified.

Then the second half, and it is the one that makes this stage worth anything:
**every row in the refusal list can be written as a check that would go red.** A
row that cannot becomes a value again, and gets deleted now rather than silently
at the verify stage.

That promise has a receiving end now. The verify stage runs
`node scripts/design.mjs refusals` and turns each row into a check; the build stage
runs `node scripts/design.mjs constraints` before writing any code. Move the record
to `confirmed` once every block is answered — that is what makes it readable to them.
A record left in `drafting` is invisible to both.

# The idea

**Open by asking: "how will we know this stage is finished?"**

Do not accept "when I've thought it through" or "when it's clear". The answer must
be an action they can perform: *"I'll read it to someone who doesn't work in tech
and they'll be able to tell me what it's for."*

If they cannot give an answer, that is the stage-1 work. Say so plainly, then help
them find one.

## The sixth sentence: does this need an agent at all?

Ask it here, in the need stage, because it is a decision about what you are building —
and because getting it wrong is the most expensive mistake available.

**One test: can you draw the decision tree?** If you can write the order of steps
and where it branches, it is a workflow and it should be built as one — fixed
sequence, one model call inside it, cheaper, faster, and far easier to check.

An agent is worth its cost when the number of possible next steps is unknown at
design time: when the right move depends on what came back last time, and you
cannot enumerate the branches in advance.

Write the answer as one line and keep it. At the design stage the flow gets re-counted, and
if the count comes back with no judgement points, this line is what tells you to
go back rather than build.

Do not accept "agents are the modern way" or "an agent sounds more capable". A
pipeline that answers correctly beats an agent that improvises and sometimes does.

## What this stage produces

One page, five sentences, each one line:

1. **Who** uses it — a person, not a market segment.
2. **When** they use it — the situation, not the frequency.
3. **Why now** — what they do instead today, and why that is worse.
4. **What they can do afterwards** that they could not before.
5. **What would tell you not to build this** — the disconfirming evidence.

The fifth is the one that saves money, and the one they will want to skip.

**And it has a trap that cost a real product its existence.** The rule is that it must
be measurable — a date, a count, a comparison. But measurable is not enough. Ask
**whose ability the signal is measuring**: a person's, or the product's. They are
different, and the first one sounds like the second.

In the second real run the signal was "if the cause cannot be determined, do not build
it", and the first answer was *"the platform data does not have it, but operations can
tell anyway."* That reads as reassurance. It is not: the judgement rested on experience,
a product cannot inherit experience, and experience cannot be written as a rule. The
signal had fired and the answer hid it.

So after they name the signal, ask **what information the judgement rests on** — and make
them point at a source:

- **A different system** (a warehouse record, the carrier's site, an email thread) —
  the signal has not fired. The first work is changing the input, not building.
- **A conversation they would have to have** — the product can do half. Say which half.
- **Experience** ("you just know") — the signal has fired. Stop.

Write the answer as *"if a person cannot point at a source, a product cannot either"*.
That sentence is the whole check, and it is cheap.

Then **two** more lines. They are answers rather than sentences, and both get left out.

**Does this need an agent at all** — `pipeline` or `agent`. One word is enough here;
the design stage redraws it properly.

**What it hands back.** The artifact, not the capability. Sentence four says what they
can *do* afterwards; this says what they *receive*. The difference is not academic:
in the first real run, an agent given only the five sentences read back the purpose and
the user correctly — the exit test passed on its own terms — and then said it had no
idea what it would get.

Write it as a noun a person could hold: "a draft reply with each sentence annotated by
the policy it rests on", not "better answers".

## How to run it

Ask one question at a time. For each, state your recommended answer first, so they
can agree or correct rather than compose from scratch:

> "I'd guess the person is a brand manager who gets a viral video forwarded in a
> group chat. Is that right, or is it someone else?"

**Sentence three is two questions, so ask it twice.** "What do you do instead today"
and "why is that worse" look like one line and are not. Asked together they collect
half an answer — the workaround, and no reason — which leaves the product with no case
for existing. Ask for the workaround; then ask for **one specific time it went wrong**,
from the last month. "It's slow" is true of everything and settles nothing.

When an answer is a feature ("it should have login", "it needs to export"), do not
accept it — ask what the person is trying to do that login or export would let them
do. Features are how people describe solutions when they have not yet said the
problem.

When an answer is a category ("an AI tool for content"), same move: ask who,
specifically, and on what day.

## The thing that goes wrong here

**You will be tempted to write this page for them.** You know what a good one looks
like, and filling in the blanks takes thirty seconds.

Do not. Every line you write is your guess about their intent, and they will
approve it because it reads well. Then at the verify stage they will have no standard to
judge against, because the standard came from you and they cannot tell whether it
is the right one.

Your job here is to **ask**, not to answer. If they say "you decide", give two
concrete options and make them pick. Do not pick for them.

**And there is a second version of the same trap, which is harder to see.** These
instructions *also* tell you to offer your recommended answer, so they can agree rather
than compose from scratch. That is right, and it is exactly how you end up writing the
page for them anyway: if they agree with every question, you cannot tell whether they
meant it or simply had nothing to object to.

Agreement on everything is a signal, not a success. When it happens, stop and ask for
one concrete fact only they can supply — the last time it went wrong, who the person is,
what the number was.

> A recommended answer that survives contact with a specific instance was theirs all
> along. One that does not was yours.

## What you record

The five sentences are a conversation until they are written down. A requirement
goes in `work/requirements/drafting/R-NNN-slug.md`: the one sentence, and what
would make it wrong.

Only when it will outlive this conversation. Something you decide and build today
does not need a file — a register full of those is a diary, and diaries are not
read.

## Exit test

They read the page to someone who does not work in tech, and that person can say back
three things: what it is for, who it is for, **and what it hands back to them.**

The third was added after the first real run. The stranger read back the first two
correctly and then said it had no idea what it would get. A test can do exactly what it
claims and still be asking about the wrong thing.

If it needs explaining, it is not done. Rewrite it shorter, not clearer — the
problem is almost always that it is describing two things.

# It can be judged

**This is the only stage that stops work outright.** Everything else can be
revisited. This one cannot be skipped, and if it cannot be completed, the honest
move is to go back to the need stage rather than forward to the ship stage.

**Open by asking: "how will we know this stage is finished?"**

The answer must be: *"I deliberately broke it, and the check told me."* Not "the
checks pass". Not "I wrote the checks".

## What this stage produces

Five to ten statements about what good and bad look like, each converted into a
check that runs without a person.

Two kinds, and you need both:

- **Countable.** Duration in a range, a required field present, no forbidden word
  used, the number of items within bounds. Cheap, stable, and where a regression
  gets caught.
- **Judgemental.** Whether the output sounds like the brand, whether a person could
  act on it. Needs a reader — a person, or a model acting as one. Expensive and
  noisier, so reserve it for what genuinely needs taste.

Countable first. Judgemental only where a countable check would be a lie.

## The five ways this stage fakes success

The first four were observed in one project; the fifth turned up in a second. All five produce a green report.

**1. A crash counts as a pass.** The check for "this must be refused" was written
as "no output was produced and the run did not succeed". A provider outage
satisfies both conditions. Three of four safety checks reported green against a
simulated 502.

*Prevention:* a check has three outcomes, not two — passed, failed, and
**could-not-be-judged**. The third is never a pass.

**2. Unimplemented checks are recorded as "skipped", and skipped counts as passed.**
The judgemental half was never built. Every run marked it skipped. The overall
verdict was "no failures, passed".

*Prevention:* a skipped check occupies a row in the report and makes the overall
verdict "incomplete". If the number of skipped checks is not printed, it is being
hidden.

**3. The check exists but was never wired into the verdict.** Implemented, unit
tested, referenced by nothing. Two of fifteen rules were in this state — and they
were the two about legal disclaimers and auditability, the two that mattered most.

*Prevention:* for each check, name the case that uses it. A check with no case is
deleted or wired, not left.

**4. The pass bar can never fail.** "At least 8 of 10 must score above 0.7" — where
the score was never computed, so the condition was vacuously true.

*Prevention:* for every threshold, ask what result would violate it. If you cannot
construct one, the threshold is decoration.

**5. The measurement changes the measurement.** Not a false signal — a signal that
is *moved by being read*. In one product, opening the dashboard added a request to
the request counter, so every look at the numbers increased them, always upward.
The same project also had pages that incremented the total and exited without
recording an outcome, so the total was larger than the sum of its parts.

*Prevention:* add the numbers up. Successes plus every named failure must equal the
total, exactly. Then load the page five times doing nothing and check that no
counter moves. Run `anb-check-reconcile`; it takes two minutes and needs nothing
but a calculator.

## Read the design record first

Before writing any check:

```bash
node scripts/design.mjs refusals
```

Each row is a concrete input and the behaviour that must replace it. Those rows are
your guardrail checks — the ones that catch a product breaking a promise to a person
rather than a function breaking its contract. They are also the easiest to leave out,
because nothing crashes when they are missing.

Three outcomes. They are not the same thing, and treating them as one is how this
stage fakes success:

- **Rows printed.** Turn each into a check. Pass an id to pin the record if more
  than one is confirmed.
- **`跳过：<reason>`.** This layer is empty by decision. Report it with the reason.
  Never report it as "nothing to refuse" — those are opposite claims.
- **Exit code 3.** No confirmed design record exists. Say so plainly, then carry on
  with the other checks. **Do not skip silently:** a guardrail layer that was never
  built must not look like one that passed.

## How to run it

1. Ask them what good looks like, in their own words. Take the first three things
   they say — those are the real criteria; the rest will be invented to fill the
   page.
2. Convert each into a check. Where you cannot, say so and mark it judgemental
   rather than pretending a countable proxy exists.
3. **Write the check before fixing the product.** If the product is fixed first,
   the check ends up describing what the product already does — which is the
   definition of a test that cannot fail.
4. Run `anb-check-break` before declaring the stage done.
5. If any check reports counts, run `anb-check-reconcile` as well — a check whose
   accounting does not add up cannot be trusted even when it says "passed".

## The thing that goes wrong here

**They will want to skip to the ship stage.** The product runs, it looks fine, and this
stage produces no visible artifact — just checks.

Say what it buys, concretely: without it, every later change is unmeasurable, and
"is this better than last week" becomes an opinion. That is the stage where products
quietly get worse for months while everyone believes they are improving.

## What you record

Every check that proves something gets an evidence file:
`work/evidence/E-NNN-slug.md` — the command, its raw output, what it proves, and
what it does not.

The last section is the one that matters. "The parser handles this shape" and "the
provider is reachable" are different claims, and a unit test only shows the first.
Leaving that section out is how a green suite comes to mean less than it looks.

Evidence is append-only. Never edit one — add another.

## Exit test

A check that was green is now red, because someone deliberately broke the product.
They saw it go red. They can name which check caught it.

If no check has ever failed, this stage is not done — regardless of how many pass.

# Manage the project's record

**Open by asking: "what are we recording — something we intend to do, or something that happened?"**

That is the fork that matters, and it is the only one. A ticket is planned work. An incident
is something that happened to you. Filing one as the other is how a ticket stops meaning
anything: it becomes half plan, half postmortem, and neither.

## Where things live

Read `work/LAYOUT.md` before answering anything about where a file goes. The rule is one
line: **if it changes state it goes in `work/`, if it does not it goes in `docs/`.**

- `work/designs/` — the four-question records from the design stage; once confirmed they
  are a spec the build and verify stages read, not a document
- `work/tickets/` — planned work, cross-session only
- `work/incidents/` — unplanned, with its own entry point
- `work/requirements/` — one sentence each, can be dropped
- `work/evidence/` — a re-runnable command and its raw output. Append-only.
- `work/receipts/` — who received what, and how they confirmed. Append-only.
- `work/artifacts/` — anything with ongoing cost: scripts, flags, dashboards, cron jobs

## The things you will be asked to do

### "The docs say N of something and I think it changed"

Run `node scripts/facts.mjs`. It prints every number the project quotes about itself,
computed from disk. Then `--check` compares the documents against those values.

Do not update the document first. The document might be right and the disk might be
surprising — `facts` tells you which. And if a number has genuinely changed, `facts` is
where the new one is derived, so the doc and the script agree by construction rather than
by remembering.

Run `node scripts/work.mjs status`. Answer from its output, not from memory.

Do not summarise it into a sentence like "things look fine". The output has a `needs you`
section for a reason: it lists things that are actually waiting. If it is empty, say so plainly.
If it is not, lead with the first item.

Two numbers in that output are worth reading aloud, because they are the ones people
quietly get wrong:

- **awaiting-verification** — work that exists but has not been proven. Not done.
- **how long something has been in-progress** — a ticket untouched for two weeks is not
  in progress, it is abandoned with extra steps.

### "Can I close this ticket?"

Check three things, in this order:

1. **Does it have evidence?** `evidence: [E-xxx]` in the frontmatter, and the file must exist.
   No evidence means no close — `work move` will refuse, and that refusal is correct.
2. **Does the evidence prove the ticket, or something adjacent?** Read the `## 这条证据能证明什么`
   and `## 不能证明什么` sections. A test suite proving the parser works does not prove the
   provider is reachable.
3. **Is there a check that has actually failed at least once?** If this ticket's work was
   verified only by things that have never gone red, the verification is unproven.

Then: `node scripts/work-move.mjs <ID> done`.

### "File this"

Pick the register using the fork above, then create the file in the right state directory.

- A ticket in `work/tickets/open/T-NNN-<slug>.md`
- An incident in `work/incidents/open/INC-NNN-<slug>.md`

The id must match the filename and must not already exist. Frontmatter carries `id`, `title`,
`stage`, `needs`. Keep the body to: what to do, completion criteria as checkboxes, why it is
still open if it is.

**Only file a ticket if the work spans sessions.** Something finished and verified inside one
conversation does not need a ticket, and creating one makes the register a diary — diaries are
not read.

### "Is this design still current?"

Read `work/designs/confirmed/`. A record that has been overtaken moves to
`superseded` with `work-move.mjs` — never edited in place, because the record of
what you decided last time is the only evidence about whether the decision was
right. `node scripts/design.mjs refusals` prints what the newest one currently says,
which is the quickest way to see whether a stage is reading a stale one.

### "Something went wrong"

That is an incident, not a ticket. `INC-` prefix, `work/incidents/open/`.

An incident records: what happened, when, what it broke, what you did, and whether it is
contained. It does not disappear when fixed — it moves to `closed` with what you learned.
Incidents are how a project remembers its own scars.

## After any change

```bash
node scripts/work.mjs check    # records are valid
node scripts/layout.mjs        # files are where LAYOUT.md says
node scripts/facts.mjs --check # numbers quoted in docs match what is on disk
```

All three must pass.

`layout` failing means a file is in the wrong home — the beginning of the duplicate problem
this structure exists to prevent.

`facts` failing means a document is quoting a number that has changed. This happens every
time something is added: the page says "15 skills", you add one, and now the page is wrong.
Nobody notices, because a stale number looks exactly like a fresh one. When `facts` reports a
mismatch, do not adjust the number until you have recounted with a second method —
`node scripts/facts.mjs` prints the values it derived from disk.

## Things you must not do

- **Do not count a record as done because the code exists.** Code existing and behaviour being
  witnessed are different facts. The tickets in this repo that say `awaiting-verification` are
  there precisely because their code is finished and their proof is missing.
- **Do not update a ticket's state by editing text.** State is the directory. Move it with the
  script, or it will disagree with itself.
- **Do not put an ADR in `work/`.** ADRs are permanent; they have no state machine. They live in
  `docs/adr/`.
- **Do not create a second home for something.** If a kind of information has a directory, use it.
  `layout` will fail, and it is right to.

## When the numbers look wrong

`check` and `layout` are the two commands that can tell you the record is broken. If a count
looks off — five tickets on disk, four reported — do not adjust the expectation. Find the
missing one. Every tool in this directory has had a bug of exactly that shape, and each was
found by comparing a count to what was on disk.

# You can see what happened

**Open by asking: "how will we know this stage is finished?"**

The answer must be: *"I broke it on purpose, and then found that failure in the
record without help."*

This stage is often needed *earlier* than its position suggests. If someone cannot
tell whether the thing is working, do this before adding features — building blind
is how a small problem becomes a rewrite.

## What to produce

Three numbers, visible without running a command:

1. **How many times it ran.** Total, and in the last day.
2. **What each run cost.** For anything that calls a model, this is the number that
   quietly grows.
3. **Why the failures failed.** Grouped by reason, not a wall of text.

Three is enough. A dashboard is not the goal; being able to answer "what happened"
at 11pm is.

## The three ways this fakes success

**1. The log records only successes.** Then "it fails sometimes" is invisible, and
the count of runs is a count of good runs. Ask what the log looks like for a failed
attempt — if the answer requires writing code, failures are not being recorded.

**2. The record is silently dropped.** A record that fails a length or format check
gets written to the log file... and rejected. The program catches the error, logs a
line to the console, and continues. The user sees "success"; the history has no
entry. In the project this was extracted from, a truncation helper returned 2006
characters against a 2000-character limit, so every long record failed to store —
and the failure was an ignored exception.

**3. The cost reads as zero.** Not "cheap" — unmeasured. A column that is always
zero looks like a well-run budget. Five run records in that project all showed
zero cost, and it was not possible to tell from them whether the number was
accurate or absent.

## How to run it

1. Decide which three questions matter. If they cannot say, use the three above.
2. Record both outcomes — success and failure — in the same place, in the same
   shape. A separate error log is a log nobody reads.
3. Record the cost of every run, even when it is zero — an explicit zero and a missing value must look different in the record.

## What you record

Anything with an ongoing cost gets an artifact record first:
`work/artifacts/active/ART-NNN-slug.md`, with an owner and a condition for
deleting it. A script, a flag, a dashboard, a scheduled job. Without the delete
condition it stays forever, and nobody later dares remove it.

Something that broke goes in `work/incidents/open/INC-NNN-slug.md`, not in a
ticket. A ticket is work you intended; an incident is something that happened. An
incident does not disappear when it is fixed — it closes, with what you learned.

## Exit test

They cause a failure deliberately, then find it in the record.

Count check: they run it three times, and the record has three entries. Then once
more with something broken, and it has four. If the numbers disagree, records are
being lost, and that is the thing to fix before anything else.

name: anb-reusable
description: The iterate stage (迭代). Take only the parts you actually used more than once and make them the starting point for the next product. Use when starting a second similar product, or when deciding what to keep.
disable-model-invocation: true
argument-hint: "What are you starting next?"
---

# The next one starts ahead

**Open by asking: "how will we know this stage is finished?"**

The answer must be: *"The second product reaches a real result faster than the
first one did."* Not "I made a template". A template that does not make the second
one faster is a cost, not an asset.

## What to change

Before deciding what to keep, decide what to change. This is the half of the stage
that closes the loop, and the half that gets skipped — carrying reusable parts
forward is satisfying, while acting on what the numbers actually said is not.

Start from the three numbers the operate stage produces: how many times it ran, what
it cost, and why the failures failed. Each implies a different kind of change, and
two of them are commonly misread:

- **It barely ran.** Not a product defect — a reach problem. No amount of building
  fixes it. Say so rather than adding features.
- **It ran and cost more than it was worth.** The fix is usually a narrower path, not
  a cheaper model.
- **It failed for one reason, repeatedly.** That reason is the next piece of work,
  and it is the only one of the three with an obvious answer.

Each decision goes back into a register, not into a summary: a requirement in
`work/requirements/` if the need itself moved, a ticket in `work/tickets/` if it is
work you are now committing to. That is what closes the loop. Without it the
observation stays in this conversation and the next round starts from memory, which
is how a project relearns the same thing every few months.

## What to keep

Only what passed all three:

1. You used it in **this** product, not in a previous one.
2. You used it **more than once**, not once with a plan to reuse.
3. It has a **check that has failed at least once** (the verify stage's rule).

Everything else is deleted. Not archived — deleted. An archive is where good
intentions go to become maintenance.

## What is usually worth keeping

- The loop that calls the model and records what happened.
- The four known-failure guards: the three-outcome check, the shared limit, the
  failure log, the isolation between two users.
- The check runner, with two example checks.
- One working example that runs.

That is roughly a day of work. It is worth a day because those four guards are the
ones nobody remembers to write.

## What is usually not worth keeping

- Multiple users, roles, permissions. You had one user. You do not know the shape of
  the problem yet.
- Multiple platforms or providers. The abstractions that make them interchangeable
  cost more than rewriting, at this size.
- A plugin system, a config file with twenty options, an interface with three
  implementations and one use.

All three are appealing because they feel like engineering. They are what slows the
second product down.

## The failure this stage exists to prevent

**The foundation built for imagined requirements.**

An agent is very good at producing a flexible, configurable, general base — and that
base becomes the heaviest thing in the next project, because every future decision
has to fit inside it.

The test is blunt: **was this used in the last product?** If not, it is a
generalisation of one case, which is a guess dressed as architecture.

## How to run it

1. List what is in the current product.
2. For each item, answer the three questions above. Most fail on (2).
3. Delete the failures. Then re-run the current product's checks to prove nothing
   broke.
4. Start the second product from what remains, and time how long until its first
   real result.

## What you record

What you decide to change goes back into the registers, not into a summary. A
requirement in `work/requirements/` if the need itself moved; a ticket in
`work/tickets/` if it is work you are now committing to.

That is what closes the loop. Without it the observation stays in this
conversation, and the next round starts from memory — which is how a project
relearns the same thing every few months.

## Exit test

Second product, first real result, faster than the first one.

If it is slower, the template is carrying weight it should not. Cut it down and
try again — do not add more to "make it more useful", which is how a template
becomes a framework.

---
name: anb-runnable
description: The build stage (开发). Build the narrowest path that takes one real input and produces one real result, with no fake data anywhere. Use when starting to build, when nothing comes out, or when the thing only works on prepared samples.
disable-model-invocation: true
argument-hint: "What should go in, and what should come out?"
---

# It runs

**Open by asking: "how will we know this stage is finished?"**

The answer must be: *"I give it an input I chose myself, and I get a result I'd show
to someone."* Not "the code is written". Not "the page loads".

## What to build

One path. Narrow. Ugly.

One real input in, one real result out. No sample data. No placeholder. No "we'll
wire the real thing later". It must run a second time and give the same kind of
result — a one-shot demo is not a path.

Deliberately excluded at this stage: login, multiple users, settings, a nice
interface, error messages for cases you haven't hit. Each of them is a way to spend
a week without learning whether the idea works.

## Read the constraints first

```bash
node scripts/design.mjs constraints
```

Two things to respect while building, both easy to break by accident:

**Judgement points stay judgement.** If the design counts three places that need a
decision at runtime, do not hard-code the common case into a special branch. That is
exactly the "works for one case" failure this stage exists to prevent, wearing the
design's authority.

**Action permissions are implementation boundaries.** Anything the design puts in the
ask-a-human tier must not be reachable without that gate. The build stage is where a
missing gate becomes invisible: nothing errors, the action simply happens.

Exit code 3 means no confirmed design. Carry on, but say so once.

## The failure this stage exists to prevent

**The demo that was never connected to anything.**

The thing will have an interface, buttons that respond, and output that looks
plausible — while the data behind it is fixed. This is not deception; it is what
happens when you build the visible half first because it is more satisfying.

The symptom is specific: **every test passes, and the first real run fails.** In the
project this method was extracted from, thirty-one unit tests were green and the
very first real analysis could not run at all, because the test fixture returned an
empty list from the one lookup that path depended on.

So at this stage, "it runs" means it ran **with input you chose**, on the **real
dependencies**, producing output **you looked at**.

## How to run it

1. Ask them for the input. One concrete example: a link, a file, a sentence they
   would actually type. Do not accept "some text".
2. Build for that input only. When you have to choose between handling a second
   case and getting the first case through, always choose the first.
3. When it runs, show them the result **and** how to run it themselves.

Do not summarise the result for them. Print it, in full, so they see what came out
rather than your description of it.

## The thing that goes wrong here

**You will reach for a framework.** "This will be easier to extend if I set up..."

No. Extending is a later problem, and a foundation built before you know the shape
of the thing is the most expensive kind of rework — it is designed to accommodate
guesses, and it will need to be torn out when the guesses are wrong.

Build the smallest thing that produces a real result. If it is one file, one file.

## What you record

Work that spans more than this conversation gets a ticket:
`work/tickets/open/T-NNN-slug.md`, saying what to do and how you will know it is
done.

Work that finishes and is verified inside one conversation does not. Opening a
ticket for it is how the register becomes a diary.

## Exit test

They run it themselves, with an input they chose, and get a result.

Then they do it a second time with an input **they did not plan for** — something
they thought of on the spot. If the second one fails, the path works for one case,
which is not the same as running.

Report honestly which of the two happened. Do not round "worked once" up to "works".

name: anb-shipable
description: The ship stage (交付). Get it to a place where someone else can open it and use it without you sitting next to them. Use when the thing works on your machine and you want to show it to someone, or before calling anything finished.
disable-model-invocation: true
argument-hint: "Who needs to use it, and on what?"
---

# Someone else can use it

**Open by asking: "how will we know this stage is finished?"**

The answer must be: *"I opened it on my phone and a person who is not me used it."*
Not "it's deployed". Not "the link works for me".

This stage exists for one reason, and it is not "going live": **it is the first time
you see the product from the position of a user.** Everything before this, you were
looking at it from the inside, where all the pieces are already in place.

## What to do

Get it to an address that opens for someone who does not have your laptop.

That is the whole requirement. Not a domain, not a certificate, not monitoring. A
link that opens elsewhere.

## The failure this stage exists to prevent

**"Works locally" reported as "ready".**

Four things are always configured on the machine where the thing was built, and
always missing everywhere else:

- the credentials (an API key in a local file)
- the data (a database that exists only there)
- the permissions (a login that only accepts one account)
- the address (a server that only listens on localhost)

None of them produce an error during development, because none of them are used
during development in their unconfigured form. They fail the moment a stranger
tries.

There is a second form worth naming: **a link that only works on their machine.** A
development address often still "opens" for its owner, so it is easy to believe it
is public. The test is not whether it opens for you.

## How to run it

1. Put it somewhere reachable.
2. List every secret and every piece of data it needs, and check each one comes
   from the environment rather than from a file on the build machine.
3. Open the address **on a device that is not the build machine** — a phone is
   best, because it is genuinely a different environment and the failures show up
   immediately.
4. Have one other person try it, and watch. Do not help them for the first minute.

Step 4 is where the information is. Whatever they get stuck on is the entire
roadmap for the next stretch of work, and it will not be what you expected.

## The thing that goes wrong here

**Filling the wait with features.** The ship stage often has dead time — a deploy, a
domain, a permission. The temptation is to add something while waiting.

Don't. Two reasons. First, unreleased features are unmeasured, and you now have a
quality bar at the verify stage that you would have to extend to cover them. Second, the
feedback from step 4 will invalidate some of what you would have built.

## What you record

Who received it, and how they confirmed, goes in `work/receipts/REC-NNN-slug.md`.
Append-only, like evidence.

This is the only register that records something outside the repository: a person
opened it and said so. Write it the same day. In a week you will not remember
whether they used it or you showed it to them.

## Exit test

They open it on a different device. It loads. One other person uses it without
instruction.

If the other person needed instruction, the gap between you and them is the product
work — not a documentation task. Write it down as a defect, not as a note.

name: native-agent-dev
description: Route an agent-product task to the right stage of this repo's workflow — from requirement clarification through spec, eval design, tracer ticket, implementation, and release. Use when starting any piece of work here, when unsure which skill applies, or when the user says "what's next", "where do I start", or "how do we build this".

# Native Agent Dev

A router over this repo's agent-product workflow. It decides **which stage** a
piece of work is in, then hands off to exactly one stage skill.

A **stage** is a gate, not a checklist item. You leave a stage when its artifact
exists and its exit test passes. Skipping a gate is allowed — but it must be a
named decision, written down in the run or the ticket, because "we skipped evals"
is the single most common reason an agent product ships feeling unfinished.

## Read this first

Before recommending a stage, read the stage skill's `SKILL.md`. The summaries
below are for orientation only, and they go stale faster than the skills do.

If the work is *not* agent-product work — a plain refactor, a dependency bump, a
pure UI bug — use the vendored skills directly instead of this router
(`/diagnosing-bugs`, `/implement`, `/code-review`). This router exists for the
work that is genuinely agent-shaped, because that work has failure modes plain
software does not.

## The stages

| # | Stage | Skill | Exits when |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Clarify | `/native-agent-dev-clarify` | The *job* is stated in the user's words, and the failure modes are named |
| 2 | Spec | `/native-agent-dev-spec` | An eval set exists and a human agrees it defines "good" |
| 3 | Ticket | `/native-agent-dev-tickets` | One tracer bullet runs end to end |
| 4 | Build | `/native-agent-dev-build` | The tracer passes its eval cases, not just its tests |
| 5 | Harden | `/native-agent-dev-eval` | Eval scores are recorded and the regression gate is wired |
| 6 | Ship | `/native-agent-dev-release` | A real user has used it and someone owns the next failure |

## How to route

Ask one question, then stop asking: **what does the user believe is blocking?**

- "I don't know what to build" / "the requirements are vague" → **1 Clarify**
- "I know what it should do, but not what good looks like" → **2 Spec**
- "The spec is agreed, where do we start coding" → **3 Ticket**
- "It's half-built and I want the next slice" → **4 Build**
- "It works in demos but not reliably" → **5 Harden**
- "It's ready, get it in front of people" → **6 Ship**

If the answer is "all of it", the first stage is 1. Always.

## The two rules that make this different from normal software

**Rule 1 — the eval is the spec.** For an agent, a prose spec is a wish. The
artifact that actually constrains behaviour is a set of input/expected-outcome
cases with a scoring rule. If stage 2 produced a spec with no eval set, it did
not finish. This is the one gate worth being pedantic about: everything
downstream measures against it, and a spec without evals means every later
argument about quality is an opinion.

**Rule 2 — the model is not the program.** When something is wrong, the first
question is *which layer*: prompt, tool contract, data, or eval. Four different
fixes, four different owners. `/native-agent-dev-build` carries the discipline for
telling them apart; do not let a run skip to "tweak the prompt" because that is
the cheapest-looking move.

## What "agent-shaped" means here

Work belongs in this flow when it has at least one of:

- A non-deterministic step whose output quality varies run to run.
- Tool calls whose *contract* (not implementation) shapes model behaviour.
- A cost or latency envelope that has to be enforced, not hoped for.
- A human in the loop who must be able to audit what happened.

If it has none of those, it is ordinary software and the vendored skills do it
better.

## Vocabulary

This repo converges on a specific set of words; use them exactly, because the
skills and the eval harness match on them.

- **Recipe** — the product artifact: a cloneable abstraction of a reference video, re-skinned for one brand.
- **Reference** — the source viral video. Its media is transient; its *analysis* is what we keep.
- **Analysis** — the structured reading of a reference (hook pattern, beats, shots, rights). Produced by exactly one tool.
- **Run** — one execution of a workflow. The unit of cost, audit, and retry.
- **Eval case** — an input plus the criteria that decide whether the output is acceptable.
- **Workflow** — a named, versioned sequence of stages the runtime executes.

`GLOSSARY.md` at the repo root is authoritative if these ever disagree.

## Where things live

```
docs/product/          product thesis and the argument for the product
docs/adr/              decisions and why they were made
docs/evals/            eval-set design and how scoring works
docs/agents/           config for the vendored engineering skills
packages/shared/       schemas the whole system agrees on — including the eval types
packages/core/         the runtime: agent loop, tool contracts, budget
packages/evals/        the eval harness and the cases themselves
apps/workbench/        the operator surface
apps/bot-gateway/      the Feishu surface
```

name: native-agent-dev-build
description: Stage 4 of the agent-product flow. Implement a ticket and, when behaviour is wrong, find the layer that is actually wrong before changing anything. Use when building a slice, or when an agent behaves badly and the instinct is to tweak the prompt.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# Stage 4 — Build

Exit test: **the ticket's behaviour passes its eval cases, not just its unit tests,
and the diff is reviewable.**

Use `/implement` for the mechanics (TDD at pre-agreed seams, typecheck often, run
the full suite once, then `/code-review`). This skill covers the part `/implement`
cannot: what to do when the *model* is the misbehaving component.

## The four layers

When an agent does the wrong thing, it is one of four layers. They have different
fixes, different owners, and wildly different costs. Guessing wrong is what turns a
one-hour fix into a two-week prompt-engineering project.

| Layer | Symptom | Fix | Bad fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Prompt** | Understands the task, but weights it wrong | Change instructions, examples | Adding more rules each time |
| **Tool contract** | Calls the right tool with the wrong arguments, or does not know when to call | Change the tool's schema or description | Telling it in the prompt to "use X for Y" |
| **Data** | Correct behaviour on correct inputs; garbage in | Fix the input, add validation | Loosening the schema until garbage passes |
| **Eval** | Output is fine but the score says otherwise | Fix the case or the rubric | Retraining the model |

**Diagnosis order: eval → data → tool → prompt.** Cheapest and most common first.
The instinct is the opposite, because prompt edits feel like progress and take one
minute to type. They also invalidate nothing you have already measured, which is
tempting and wrong.

## Diagnosing: the concrete procedure

1. **Reproduce as an eval case.** If you cannot make a failing case, you do not
   understand the failure yet. Do not fix what you cannot reproduce.
2. **Read the run's steps, in order.** What did the model actually see at the
   moment it went wrong? Most "the model is dumb" bugs are "the tool returned
   something confusing" or "the schema let a bad value through".
3. **Check the tool boundary first.** Did each tool return what the model needed,
   in a form it could act on? An error message the model cannot act on costs a turn
   and often produces a worse retry.
4. **Only then look at the prompt.** And when you do, change *one* thing, and re-run
   the whole eval set — not just the failing case. Prompt edits are the only change
   in this system that can silently break cases you were not looking at.

## Writing the code

- **Ports at the boundary.** Tools depend on interfaces (`BrandStore`,
  `VisionAnalyzer`), not on Prisma/Drizzle clients. This is what makes the eval
  harness able to run the real tool code with fake data.
- **Never throw from a tool.** Return `{ isError: true }`. A throw kills the run.
  `packages/core/src/tools/result.ts` gives you the shape; use it, do not re-invent
  it per tool.
- **Budget is enforced in the loop, not the prompt.** A prompt saying "be concise"
  is not a cost control. `maxBudgetUsd` plus an in-loop check is.
- **Every run persists its steps.** If a run cannot be explained after the fact,
  it is not debuggable, and agent bugs are notoriously non-reproducible.
- **Schemas validate at the boundary.** The model's output is untrusted input. A
  malformed recipe must fail at the schema, loudly, not become a weird card in the
  review queue.

## Testing: two different jobs

Both are required, and confusing them is common.

**Unit and integration tests** verify your code. They run in CI, must be fast, and
never call a model. The step-mapping function, the budget arithmetic, the schema
validation, the tool error paths — all of these are ordinary code with ordinary
tests.

**Eval runs** verify the agent's judgement. They call the model, cost money, and
are therefore *not* in the fast CI path. Run them when behaviour changed:
after a prompt edit, a tool-schema change, a model upgrade, or a data-shape change.

A ticket is not done when its unit tests pass. It is done when its eval cases pass.

## When the model genuinely cannot do it

Sometimes all four layers are fine and the task is simply beyond the current model
at acceptable cost. Before concluding that:

- Check whether the task can be decomposed — three focused calls often beat one
  ambitious one, and fail more explainably.
- Check whether a deterministic step can replace a generative one. Anything with a
  right answer should be code, not a model.
- Check whether the deliverable was too ambitious for this ticket. A weaker
  artifact that ships beats a stronger one that never converges.

Then write it down in the ADR. "We tried to have the model do X and it could not,
so we do Y" is one of the most valuable documents in an agent codebase, because it
stops the next person from re-litigating it.

## Exit checklist

- [ ] The failing behaviour is reproducible as an eval case
- [ ] Unit tests pass; the change is typechecked
- [ ] The ticket's eval cases pass, run against the real model
- [ ] No tool throws; failures are values
- [ ] The full eval set was re-run, not just the changed case
- [ ] `/code-review` has run on the diff
- [ ] Any "the model cannot do this" conclusion is recorded in an ADR

Then: `/native-agent-dev-eval` when the slice needs hardening, or the next ticket
from the frontier.

name: native-agent-dev-clarify
description: Stage 1 of the agent-product flow. Turn a vague agent idea into a stated job, named failure modes, and a decision about whether an agent is even the right shape. Use when requirements are unclear, when someone says "we should build an agent that...", or before any spec is written.

# Stage 1 — Clarify

Exit test: **the job is stated in the user's words, every failure mode is named,
and a human has agreed the agent is the right shape for this problem.**

Two of those three are the usual suspects. The third — "is this even an agent" —
is the one that saves the most money, so it goes first.

## Step 1: Decide whether this should be an agent

An agent earns its cost only when all four are true:

1. **The path varies.** Different inputs need different sequences of steps. If every
   request follows the same fixed pipeline, that is a workflow, and a workflow
   should be code — cheaper, faster, testable.
2. **The steps are discoverable at runtime.** The system cannot enumerate them in
   advance. If it can, write the enumeration.
3. **A tool surface exists.** The agent acts through tools you own. A chat box with
   no tools is a prompt, and prompts belong in a single API call.
4. **Errors are recoverable.** A wrong tool call can be detected and retried. If a
   single mistake is unrecoverable, you want a form with validation, not an agent.

If fewer than four hold, say so plainly and propose the non-agent design. This is
not a formality — the most common product failure in this space is an agent where
a form would have been better, shipped because agents are interesting.

For this repo's product specifically: the TikTok recipe workflow clears all four.
The reference is unstructured, the analysis path depends on what the video
contains, the tools are ours (analyse, save, draft), and a bad draft is caught by
review before it ships. If you cannot restate that argument for the work in front
of you, stop and ask.

## Step 2: Get the job in the user's words

Interview them — use the vendored `/grilling` primitive via `/grill-with-docs` if
they want the full treatment. What you need out of it, at minimum:

- **Who** does this today, and what do they actually do instead? "Nobody does this"
  is usually wrong; someone does it in a spreadsheet or by hand, and *that* is your
  competitor.
- **What does done look like to them**, in their vocabulary, not ours.
- **What would make them stop using it** in week two. This question surfaces the
  real quality bar far better than "what features do you want".
- **What must never happen.** For brand content: an unsubstantiated health claim,
  a competitor's asset, a rights violation. These become guardrails, and they are
  cheaper to collect now than to discover in a review queue later.

Write the result to `docs/product/<feature>-brief.md`. Keep it under a page —
if it needs more, the job is not clear yet.

## Step 3: Name the failure modes

Every agent product fails in a handful of characteristic ways. Name which ones
apply *before* design, because each one becomes a specific test in stage 2.

| Failure mode | What it looks like | Where it gets caught |
|---|---|---|
| **Wrong shape** | It answers a question nobody asked | Clarify (here) — cheap to fix |
| **Silent drift** | Output is plausible but off-brand or off-brief | Eval case with a rubric |
| **Tool misuse** | Calls the right tool with wrong arguments | Tool contract + eval case |
| **Confident wrongness** | Asserts a claim it cannot support | Guardrail + eval case |
| **Cost blowout** | One user runs a $40 tab | Runtime budget, not a prompt |
| **Unexplainable run** | "It gave me something weird yesterday" | Run steps, persisted |
| **Context rot** | Quality degrades over a long conversation | Session design |

For each applicable row, write one sentence: *how we would notice*. A failure
mode with no detection story is not a failure mode, it is a wish.

## Step 4: Confirm the artefact the product delivers

Agents are judged by what they hand back, not by their transcript. Decide the
deliverable shape now — for this repo it is a **Recipe**: a structured object a
human reviews and a shooter acts on. If the deliverable is "a chat response", say
that out loud, because it is a much weaker product and it changes the eval design
significantly.

## Exit checklist

- [ ] The four agent-shape criteria are argued, not assumed
- [ ] The job is written in the user's vocabulary, under one page
- [ ] "What would make them stop using it" has a concrete answer
- [ ] "What must never happen" is a list, not a vibe
- [ ] Each applicable failure mode has a detection story
- [ ] The deliverable's shape is named
- [ ] `docs/product/<feature>-brief.md` exists and a human has read it

Then: `/native-agent-dev-spec`.

name: native-agent-dev-eval
description: Stage 5 of the agent-product flow. Turn "seems to work" into measured, regression-gated quality — run the eval set, read scores honestly, and wire a gate that fails when quality drops. Use before shipping, after a model or prompt change, or when quality feels inconsistent.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# Stage 5 — Harden

Exit test: **scores are recorded, the gate is wired, and the numbers are honest.**

"Honest" is doing real work in that sentence. Most eval suites in agent products
are worse than none, because a suite that always passes teaches the team to ignore
it, and then a real regression ships unnoticed.

## Run it

```
pnpm --filter @mas/evals eval            # full set
pnpm --filter @mas/evals eval --case <id>  # one case
```

Record every run to `packages/evals/runs/<date>-<label>.json` and commit it. A
score with no history cannot answer the only question that matters: *did this
change make it worse?*

## Read the scores honestly

Four questions, in order:

1. **Is any `should_fail` case passing that should not?** A guardrail that stops
   firing is a ship-blocker, regardless of every other number. Check this first,
   always.
2. **Which cases went down since the last run, and does the diff explain it?** A
   drop with no explanation is a regression even if the total improved.
3. **Is the total moving for the right reason?** Ten cases at 0.71 passing a 0.7
   bar is not the same as five at 0.95 and five at 0.45 — and the mean hides it.
   Look at the distribution, not the average.
4. **Is the judge agreeing with humans?** Sample two outputs the judge scored well
   and one it scored badly, and read them yourself. If you disagree, the rubric is
   wrong, and every number downstream is noise.

## The traps

**The flaky threshold.** If the same commit scores 0.68 then 0.74, the bar is
inside the noise. Either widen the case set until the variance is understood, or
pick a bar with margin. Never lower the bar to make a run pass — that is how a gate
becomes decoration.

**The judge that got easier.** Changing a judge prompt to be "fairer" is
indistinguishable from making it more lenient, and it silently recalibrates every
past score. Treat a judge-prompt change like a data migration: re-score the
previous run's outputs and state the delta before accepting it.

**The case that grew**. A case edited to accommodate a new behaviour is fine; a
case edited to accommodate a *worse* behaviour is a bar being lowered through a
side door. Read the diff on eval cases as carefully as the diff on code.

**The unrun suite.** An eval suite that only runs when someone remembers is not a
gate. It belongs in CI on the paths that can affect quality (prompt, tools, model
config, schemas) — and those runs must cost an amount you are willing to pay on
every PR. If they are too expensive, evaluate a subset per PR and the full set
nightly. Decide which, write it down, and wire it.

## Design the gate

A gate is a rule in CI that turns a quality drop into a red build. Minimum viable:

- Runs on every PR that touches `packages/core`, `packages/shared`, `packages/evals`, or a prompt.
- Fails if any `should_fail` case regresses. Non-negotiable.
- Fails if the deterministic pass rate drops below the recorded baseline.
- Warns (does not fail) on rubric-score drops, with the delta printed so the
  reviewer can judge.

Warning on rubric drops rather than failing is deliberate. Judge scores have
noise; a hard gate on a noisy signal gets muted within a month, and a muted gate is
worse than a soft one that stays on.

## Cost discipline

Eval runs are the largest recurring bill in most agent products. Keep it visible:

- Record cost per run alongside scores. A quality gain that quintuples the eval
  bill is a product decision, not an engineering one — surface it.
- Cache aggressively at the fixture level: tool responses that are fake should be
  hard-coded, never re-fetched.
- Separate the cheap deterministic check (schema validity, banned terms — free)
  from the expensive judge pass. Run the cheap one on every commit; the expensive
  one per PR.

## Exit checklist

- [ ] Full eval set run, results committed to `packages/evals/runs/`
- [ ] No `should_fail` case passing when it should not be
- [ ] Score deltas vs. the previous run explained
- [ ] Two high-scoring and one low-scoring output read by a human
- [ ] The gate is wired in CI and its cost is known
- [ ] Baseline recorded, with the date and the model version it was measured on

Then: `/native-agent-dev-release`.

# Stage 6 — Ship

Exit test: **a real user has used it on real work, and someone owns the next
failure.**

Shipping an agent is different from shipping software in one specific way: it
keeps making new decisions after you deploy it. So the release checklist here is
weighted toward *observability and control*, not toward the deploy itself.

## The five things that must be true before a real user touches it

**1. Cost has a ceiling, enforced in code.** Not a dashboard, not an alert. A run
that crosses `maxCostUsd` stops. Know the number per run, and know the worst case
per day (runs × ceiling). If that worst case is unacceptable, lower the ceiling
before launch, not after.

**2. Every run is reconstructable.** The steps, the tool calls, the token counts,
the cost, the model version, the workflow version. When a user says "it gave me
something weird on Tuesday", you need to answer without asking them to reproduce.

**3. Failure is visible to the user, not just to you.** A failed run must say what
happened and whether retrying helps. An agent that silently returns nothing is
indistinguishable from one that is broken — and users forgive the first, not the
second.

**4. The guardrails are enforced at the tool layer.** Not in the prompt. A brand's
prohibited claims must be impossible to persist, not merely discouraged. Verify by
trying: run a `should_fail` case against production config.

**5. A named owner for the next failure.** Not "the team". A person. Agent products
degrade in ways that are invisible in aggregate metrics but obvious to the person
using them, so someone has to be reading the feedback.

## The surfaces

Two, with different jobs — resist the temptation to make one do both.

**The bot** (Feishu) is where the work happens. It meets users where they already
are, which is why it gets used. Keep it narrow: it does the workflow, it does not
have settings.

**The workbench** is where the work is supervised. Reviewing recipes, checking runs,
adjusting brand guardrails, reading eval scores. It is used by fewer people, more
deliberately. Its value is entirely in making the agent's behaviour legible — a
workbench that only shows a chat log is a chat app with extra steps.

The split matters because it decides where a feature goes. "Configure the brand
voice" is workbench. "Make a video from this link" is the bot. Anything that is
both is a workbench feature with a bot shortcut.

## Pilot, not launch

Ship to one brand, with a person who will tell you the truth. What you are
measuring in a pilot is not conversion — it is:

- What do they use it for that you did not anticipate?
- What do they do *after* it gives them a recipe? (The handoff is where products
  die: a recipe nobody can shoot is a failed product even if the recipe is great.)
- Which outputs do they rewrite, and does the rewrite pattern suggest a missing
  tool or a bad rubric?

Every rewrite is an eval case waiting to be written. Collect them daily for the
first two weeks; that single habit is the difference between a product that
improves and one that plateaued at launch quality.

## Versioning

Two versions matter in an agent product, and conflating them makes incidents
unreadable:

- **Workflow version** — what the agent was asked to do. Store it on every run.
- **Model version** — what was doing the asking. Store it on every run.

A quality drop is usually one of these two changing. Without both recorded, the
first question of every incident ("what changed?") has no cheap answer.

## Rollback

Know the answer before launch: if quality craters, what do you revert, and how long
does it take? For prompts and tool schemas, it is a commit. For a model upgrade, it
is a config change — and it must be possible *without* a deploy, or a bad model
rollout becomes a bad week.

## Exit checklist

- [ ] Cost ceiling enforced in code; worst case per day known
- [ ] Run reconstruction works: pick a random run, explain it
- [ ] Failure messages are actionable for a non-engineer
- [ ] Every guardrail verified against production config, not just in tests
- [ ] Workflow version and model version stored on every run
- [ ] One named owner for feedback, and a place the feedback lands
- [ ] One real user on one real brand, with a check-in scheduled for day 3 and day 10
- [ ] Rollback path known and rehearsed once

## After this

The loop does not end here. Every rewrite a user makes becomes a case in
`packages/evals`, which re-enters the flow at stage 2 for the next iteration. That
cycle — pilot, collect rewrites, add cases, improve — is the product. The initial
build is just the thing that gets the cycle started.
